lines.text: Quick recap. A fishing crew in the Ross Sea hauled up a squid of about half a tonne, one of the biggest ever seen, and nobody could say much about how it lived.
In nineteen twenty five, scientists were looking through the stomach of a sperm whale, and they found two pieces of arms from a squid nobody could name.
That was it. Just two arm crowns. From those, they described a brand new animal and called it the colossal squid.
And for a long time, that was how we learned about it. Bits and pieces, found inside the animals that eat it.
Sperm whales eat squid, and a squid has one hard part that a whale cannot digest, its beak.
So beaks pile up in the whale's stomach, and scientists can read them like a record of what the whale has been eating.
Beaks from sperm whale stomachs have been measured at up to forty nine millimeters, bigger than the beak of the 2003 specimen, which was thirty eight.
Think about what that means. The whales are eating squid bigger than the ones we have ever managed to catch.
Since that first find, in about a hundred years, fewer than ten adult sized colossal squid have ever been reported.
A hundred years of searching, and you could count the adult sized ones on your fingers.
Most of them came from dead or dying animals, found in whale stomachs, in seabird stomachs, or on toothfish lines.
So now we have a body, and we know a whale can eat it. But there is one part of this animal that makes scientists stop and stare.
